LAS removal of 9.0 ± 2.4% was 
obtained with the co-substrate 
mixture. Increasing co-substrate 
complexity increased LAS removal, 
reaching up to 50% with yeast 
extract supplementation.
In the present study, ethanol resulted in LAS 
removals of 19.2 ± 3.2% and 20.8 ± 4.1% in the 
anaerobic and microaerated reactors, 
respectively. Sucrose alone increased removal 
to 25.8% in the anaerobic reactor and 34.3% in 
the microaerated reactor under an HRT of 8 h.

Anaerobic treatment 
with nitrate, sulfate,

Bacillota was predominant in the 
microbial community. 
Pseudomonadota was also reported 
as an abundant phylum in anaerobic 
systems treating surfactant-
containing wastewater, particularly 
with sucrose as a co-substrate.
Bacillota predominated in the ethanol-fed 
reactors of the present study. After sucrose 
addition, Pseudomonadota became dominant, 
particularly in the microaerated reactor, 
coinciding with increased LAS removal.

conditions
Parabens
Microaeration
An airflow of 4 mL·min⁻¹ increased 
contaminant removal to 90–94%, 
compared with less than 30% under 
strictly anaerobic conditions. 
Microaeration improved treatment 
performance but compromised 
methane purity.
The present study also showed that 
microaeration could improve contaminant 
removal while decreasing methane 
concentration in the biogas. However, the 
improvement in LAS removal depended 
strongly on the co-substrate and was significant 
only when sucrose was supplied.

Higher LAS removal was obtained 
with ethanol than with the sucrose–
ethanol mixture.
The opposite tendency was observed in the 
present study, in which sucrose promoted 
higher LAS removal than ethanol. This

difference may be associated with reactor 
configuration and operating conditions.

Microaeration enhanced organic 
matter removal but compromised 
methane purity.
A similar behavior was observed in the present 
study. Methane concentrations were lower in 
the microaerated reactor, averaging 36.6% with 
ethanol and 32.7% with sucrose, although 
volumetric methane production was maintained 
or increased.

A high abundance of Bacillota was

Bacillota also predominated in the ethanol-fed

Ethanol or sucrose at

0.1 L O₂·Lfeed⁻¹·d⁻¹; 
HRT of 8 h
With ethanol, LAS removal was 
19.2 ± 3.2% in the UASB reactor 
and 20.8 ± 4.1% in the UMSB 
reactor, with no significant 
difference. With sucrose, removal 
increased to 25.8% and 34.3%, 
respectively. Microaeration with 
sucrose promoted a less diverse but 
more specialized community 
associated with Pleomorphomonas, 
Desulfovibrio, oxidative pathways, 
sulfur metabolism, and maintenance 
of methanogenic functions.
The combined use of sucrose and microaeration 
provided the highest LAS removal. Unlike the 
previous studies discussed in the manuscript, 
the present work jointly evaluated co-substrate 
selection, controlled microaeration, reactor 
performance, methane production, microbial 
community structure, and predicted metabolic 
pathways related to LAS transformation.
Abbreviations: COD, chemical oxygen demand; HRT, hydraulic retention time; LAS, linear alkylbenzene sulfonate; UASB, upflow anaerobic 
sludge blanket; UMSB, upflow microaerobic sludge blanket.
